First Cloud AI Journey: Notes from a Morning of Demos Event: First Cloud AI Journey
Date: October 24, 2026
Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
Role: Attendee
I attended the First Cloud AI Journey meetup to hear how local engineering teams are moving cloud and AI ideas into working systems. Five short sessions made the morning feel like a tour through different parts of the same problem: making AI useful while keeping the surrounding system secure and manageable.
Sessions that changed how I think The Vietnamese Voice AI demonstration made latency tangible. A voice assistant has to listen, interpret, respond, and sound natural within a conversation. A model that is accurate but pauses too long can still feel broken to its user. In the demo, an AI system made a real phone call and conducted an initial Vietnamese-language screening interview for a cloud engineer role. Seeing speech AI handle a live interaction helped me connect model capability with the full user experience.
The two security sessions showed that agents and infrastructure need boundaries before they receive autonomy. One covered cross-account access in AWS Organizations; another described scanning Infrastructure-as-Code during pull requests and testing staging systems with an adversarial user persona. I took away a practical rule: decide what an AI tool is allowed to read or change before connecting it to real resources.
The AgentCore session introduced short-term and long-term memory for production agents. The closing discussion added the operational details: track token use by component, remove stale context, and prevent an agent from taking destructive actions. These details made “agent memory” feel less like a feature and more like a design responsibility.
What I plan to apply As an AI student, I used to judge an agent mainly by whether its answer looked good. I now want to judge it by latency, tool permissions, cost per task, and what happens when it makes a mistake. For my own coding assistant, I will start with read-only permissions, keep secrets out of the repository, and add logs before experimenting with automated changes.
The meetup also reminded me to learn from production examples, not only tutorials. My next step is to build a small agent workflow with explicit limits and record its behavior across successful and failed runs. That should teach me more than adding another tool integration without measuring its effect.

title: Blog 1
content:
Automating Medical Coding with AWS Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Medical coding is the process of translating free-text clinical phrases such as “migrane” (misspelled) or “flutters in my chest sometimes” into standardized codes from dictionaries like MedDRA (adverse events) and WHODrug (medications). It is safety-critical—a single wrong code can route an event into the wrong safety signal—yet largely repetitive and traditionally reviewed term by term by human coders. Handing the entire workflow over to an autonomous agent makes the execution path dependent on model reasoning, making it difficult to review and reproduce.
AWS presents a reference pattern that resolves this tension by letting a deterministic workflow control the execution order while constraining the agent to make judgments inside a bounded step.
Core Architecture Components AWS Step Functions: Orchestrates the pipeline (Standard Workflow), with each execution processing a single term and preserving full execution history for auditing. AWS Lambda: Executes deterministic processing steps (CheckDirect, WriteBack, and MCP tool handlers). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness & Gateway: Runs the coding agent and exposes two MCP tools: search_dictionary and get_study_info. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector: Stores reference dictionaries and vector embeddings in a single database. Amazon Bedrock: Provides Claude Sonnet 5 for agent reasoning and Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 for semantic retrieval. Cost-Optimized Execution Flow The pipeline follows a cost-first escalation strategy—resolving simple cases with the lowest-cost deterministic mechanism before invoking an LLM:
Direct Lookup: Matches the input against predefined dictionary entries or synonym lists (via the CheckDirect Lambda function) using exact or synonym matching, resolving straightforward cases in the first step without calling an LLM. Agentic Invocation: Triggered only when direct lookup fails. The Coding Agent (running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) analyzes the term, retrieves dictionary candidates, and queries study context through MCP tools to disambiguate complex phrases. Route on Confidence Score: Decisions are routed based on the agent’s confidence score: 0.90 or higher: Automatically accept and code the term. 0.70 to below 0.90: Route to human-in-the-loop review. Below 0.70: Keep open for further review. Outcome Persistence: Before persisting data (via the WriteBack Lambda function), the system verifies that the selected code exists in the dictionary and stores the full hierarchy path alongside a concise explanation of the agent’s reasoning. Why Confidence-Based Routing Beats Raw Embedding Similarity One of the strongest aspects of this design is routing on agent confidence rather than raw embedding similarity alone:
“migrane” scored only 0.37 in embedding similarity yet 0.97 in agent confidence, whereas “flutters in my chest sometimes” scored 0.65 in similarity but only 0.75 in confidence—embedding similarity alone would have ranked these two cases in the wrong order. The identical phrase “cramps” was coded as “muscle spasms” (0.92, auto-coded) in an oncology study and “abdominal pain” (0.85, routed to human review) in a reflux study because the agent read the study description via get_study_info. Caveats & Practical Notes Reference sample only: Not validated for clinical use; requires benchmarking against a labeled ground-truth dataset to measure accuracy and auto-coding error rates before production adoption. Confidence score variance across runs: Across six runs of the oncology “cramps” case, confidence ranged from 0.75 to 0.92 (2 auto-coded, 4 routed to review), though the selected code remained identical. Testing should evaluate the chosen code and account for score variance below 0.90. Retrieval limits agent selection: Because “Palpitations” ranked 19th in retrieval, the agent never considered it. The article recommends hybrid retrieval to improve candidate recall. Licensing & compliance: MedDRA and WHODrug require commercial licenses, and handling protected health information requires signing a BAA for HIPAA-eligible AWS services. Cost driver: The largest cost component is the Aurora Serverless v2 cluster (minimum 0.5 ACU, billed even while idle); the article does not publish an exact total cost estimate. Scope boundary: This pattern is not suited for open-ended conversational workflows where the agent itself must decide arbitrary next steps. Key Takeaway I read this article to study a clean architectural separation: delegate judgment to the AI agent, while keeping execution order, confidence thresholds, and audit trails firmly under workflow control.
Source: Automate medical coding with Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Sachin Doshi, Andrei Maksimov, Rostislav Markov, AWS Architecture Blog (October 21, 2026)

title: Blog 2
content:
Upgrading AI-Powered Game Backends with New Amazon DynamoDB Features When integrating AI into games, the hardest engineering challenge is often not choosing the model, but choosing the state-storage infrastructure. A generative NPC that forgets every prior conversation, an AI dungeon master that loses the quest storyline mid-session, or an agent that loses state after an AWS Lambda cold start all share the same root cause: the lack of a durable, globally consistent state layer.
The AWS for Games Blog post highlights that Amazon DynamoDB—already widely used in game backends for player profiles, inventories, leaderboards, and session state—now introduces four enhancements tailored for AI-powered game workloads.
Four Key Amazon DynamoDB Enhancements Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC): Writes are synchronously replicated to at least one other Region before returning success, so reading with ConsistentRead=True from any replica returns the latest version. Under the hood, it uses a three-node multi-Region journal that commits once two of the three nodes confirm. The trade-off is single-digit millisecond additional latency, making it suitable for premium currency balances and agent checkpoints. Zero-ETL to Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse: DynamoDB automatically replicates table data to Lakehouse in Apache Iceberg format using incremental CDC synchronization (typically within minutes) without consuming production read capacity—replacing the traditional six-service pipeline (Streams, Lambda/Glue, S3, Glue Data Catalog, Athena). LangGraph DynamoDBSaver: Persists agent checkpoints and state (conversation history, tool outputs, NPC relationship scores, quest context) keyed by each player session’s thread_id. Payloads exceeding 350 KB are automatically offloaded to Amazon S3. Pricing Reductions: Effective November 1, 2024, on-demand throughput pricing was reduced by 50% and Global Tables replication write pricing by up to 67%. Reference Architecture Summary The blog combines all four features into a reference design:
Single-table design with partition key player_id and sort key record_type. Dedicated MRSC tables per Region set, using strong consistency (ConsistentRead=True) for premium currency and agent checkpoints, and eventual consistency for leaderboards. Zero-ETL enabled on the game-session table to retrain personalization models weekly in SageMaker Lakehouse. On-demand capacity mode with warm throughput pre-configured to 2× expected peak ahead of major in-game events. Caveats & Critical Observations MRSC feature limitations: MRSC does not support TTL, Local Secondary Indexes (LSI), or transactional operations (TransactWriteItems, TransactGetItems). Data expiration must be handled manually via conditional writes or cleanup Lambda functions. Regional-set boundary: MRSC only operates within regional sets (US, Europe, Asia-Pacific) and does not yet provide cross-continent strong consistency. Studios with global players should use MRSC per regional set and accept eventual consistency for global leaderboards. Zero-ETL prerequisites: Enabling zero-ETL requires turning on Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) on the source table and granting permissions to AWS Glue. Cost example discrepancy: The article cites 10 million writes per day across two replicas with pricing dropping from ~$1.25 to $0.625 per million WRUs, yet claims ~$6,250/month in savings. Recalculating from those exact figures yields only about $375/month, so teams should compute savings against their own actual traffic volumes. Lack of empirical benchmarks: The post describes architecture only and does not include measured latency, cost, or player-experience metrics. Diagram vs. text nuance: While the diagram refers to a “single-table design,” it marks game-session records as outside MRSC—making it most logical to interpret game-session data as residing in a separate table serving as the zero-ETL source. Key Takeaway I read this post to study a core design principle for AI in games: the quality of an NPC or AI agent’s player experience depends heavily on durable, consistent state persistence, not just the underlying model.
Source: Level up your AI-powered game backend with Amazon DynamoDB new features — Naveen Kantamneni, Jackie Jiang, AWS for Games Blog (October 21, 2026)

title: Proposal
content:
AWS Plant Disease Detection Project Proposal Twelve week implementation and validation plan 16 October 2026 | Sydney | ap-southeast-2
We propose a twelve-week implementation and validation program for a containerized tomato leaf classification application on EC2, S3 and CloudWatch. The plan starts from the existing prototype and closes deployment, evidence and operational gaps.
1 Executive summary The project will deliver a reproducible AWS demonstration with a responsive frontend, CPU inference API, privately stored model artifacts and basic CloudWatch observability. GitHub Actions will publish images; a controlled manual procedure will deploy and roll back compatible image and model versions. This scope fits a backend and MLOps learning project without requiring serverless or microservices claims.
The project budget follows the low-traffic AWS demonstration configuration in the project overview: USD 50 per month before tax, or USD 150 for three monthly billing periods covering the twelve-week project. With USD 200 in eligible AWS credits, four months of this configuration are covered. Credit availability and expiration depend on the account. [6–12]
2 Problem statement A locally trained classifier is difficult to reproduce on another host when model weights, class ordering, preprocessing and dependencies are managed separately. LAN-only access limits demonstrations, and an apparently healthy process may still fail prediction because of missing weights, CORS, queue saturation or permission errors. Source-code synchronization alone does not update a running container.
The project therefore needs a versioned release identity, least-privilege access to artifacts, evidence of real inference on AWS, actionable host monitoring and a documented recovery process. The current prototype supplies working components, but it does not yet establish high availability, field accuracy or automated production deployment.
3 Solution architecture AWS services used Service Role Design choice Amazon EC2 Run frontend and API containers One x86_64 host in Sydney Amazon S3 Store checkpoint and class map Private versioned artifacts Amazon CloudWatch Container logs, host metrics, and dashboard 60 second Agent metrics; 7 day logs IAM and VPC Identity and network controls Instance role and source IP rules Component design The browser reaches Next.js on port 3000 and FastAPI on port 8000 at the same EC2 hostname. FastAPI loads a MobileNet checkpoint once per process and validates the supplied class map. Prediction and Grad-CAM++ share a bounded execution slot. S3 is accessed at deployment time; uploaded user images do not need to be persisted in S3 for the current use case.
GitHub Actions -> GHCR -> manual deployment to EC2 Private S3 artifacts -> host version directory -> read-only API mount Browser -> Next.js frontend and FastAPI API Container logs + Agent metrics -> CloudWatch dashboard The architecture deliberately uses a public subnet with restricted inbound access for the demonstration. S3 VPC endpoints, on-premises connectivity, DNS simulation, load balancing and autoscaling are outside the baseline. A private-network extension can be evaluated later without being reported as an implemented feature.
4 Technical implementation Build the frontend with its existing multi-stage Dockerfile and standalone Next.js output. Build the API with Dockerfile.deploy so the checkpoint remains outside the image. CI gates include Python tests, frontend build, backend build and frontend container smoke tests. Publish both images with full commit tags and record digests; tests using fixture weights remain distinct from real-model acceptance tests.
Create the EC2 instance profile with scoped GetObject permission and CloudWatch delivery permissions. Download model artifacts from mobilenet-distilled-v1 and compare SHA256 values before mounting them read-only. Bind the API and frontend ports, configure CORS_ORIGINS with the exact page origin and use restart unless-stopped. Recreate containers when changing image or environment settings.
Validate readiness, real-image prediction, response schema and model identity. Then validate browser upload and Grad-CAM++ on desktop and phone. Measure API latency under a declared request count and concurrency instead of interpreting a single request as p95. Evaluate macro F1 and per-class recall only when an independent labeled dataset is available; do not promise a diagnostic accuracy without that evaluation.
Use CloudWatch Logs for both containers and CloudWatch Agent metrics for host memory and disk, with seven-day log retention. Review the host dashboard during operation. Record rollback and EC2 stop/start rehearsals, including public IP and CORS updates.
5 Timelines and milestones Each week receives 20 planned working hours, totaling 240 hours. The proposed schedule runs from September 7 through November 27, 2026, with November 27 as the final working day, ahead of the November 30 cutoff. This is a planned schedule, not a reconstruction of dates already worked. AWS operating costs follow the monthly configuration in the budget below; they are not calculated from the planned working hours.
Week and target dates Work package Milestone evidence 1 · Sep 7–11 Scope and acceptance criteria Architecture scope agreed 2 · Sep 14–18 Audit model preprocessing and labels Artifact manifest and hashes 3 · Sep 21–25 Harden API validation and errors API contract and tests 4 · Sep 28–Oct 2 Validate frontend and explanations Browser workflow verified locally 5 · Oct 5–9 Package demo containers Two images pass smoke tests 6 · Oct 12–16 Complete CI and GHCR delivery Published release digests 7 · Oct 19–23 Prepare AWS IAM network and budget EC2 role and restricted connectivity 8 · Oct 26–30 Store and retrieve S3 artifacts Download hashes match 9 · Nov 2–6 Deploy EC2 and test real inference Desktop and phone acceptance 10 · Nov 9–13 Configure CloudWatch observability Log groups, host metrics, and dashboard checked 11 · Nov 16–20 Rehearse rollback and measure latency Recovery and performance evidence 12 · Nov 23–27 Finalize report demo and cleanup Handover and cost review 6 Cost The approved low-traffic demonstration budget for Sydney (ap-southeast-2) is USD 50 per month before tax. It covers one t3.medium EC2 host running 730 hours per month, a 20 GiB gp3 volume, one public IPv4 address, small S3 model artifacts, and low-volume monitoring. The monthly allocation is:
Service / usage Monthly cost EC2 Linux t3.medium, 730 hours $38.54 EBS gp3, 20 GiB $1.60 Public IPv4, 730 hours $3.65 S3 model checkpoint and class map $0.01 CloudWatch logs, host metrics, and dashboard $0.00 Internet data transfer within the 100 GB/month shared allowance $0.00 Operating headroom $6.20 Monthly total $50.00 The twelve-week project reserves three monthly billing periods, for a total project budget of USD 150 before tax. Eligible AWS credits of USD 200 cover four months at this monthly budget, leaving USD 50 for the twelve-week period. Credit eligibility, available balance, and expiration depend on the AWS account; confirm them in the Billing Console. Configure a monthly budget alert and review gross usage regularly, since budget notifications do not stop resources automatically. [6–12]
This budget covers a single host and low-traffic demo use. It excludes tax, GPU training, load balancing, NAT Gateway, databases, high availability, traffic beyond the stated allowance, excess logs or metrics, and T3 CPU-credit surcharges. Training and research runs use a local machine; GHCR and GitHub Actions remain within included account usage. Stopping EC2 reduces compute charges, while EBS storage remains billable. Check the AWS Pricing Calculator if the region or configuration changes. [6–10]
7 Risk assessment Risk Likelihood and impact Mitigation and owner Credit depletion Medium / High Operator stops EC2 and reviews gross costs weekly Instance capacity or plan restriction Medium / Medium Operator checks eligible x86_64 type and revises budget Incorrect model or class order Medium / High ML developer verifies hashes map and preprocessing CORS or public IP change High / Medium Backend operator recreates container with correct origin Access or credential exposure Medium / High Operator uses instance role private S3 and restricted SSH Host outage or saturation Medium / High Backend operator measures queue load and rehearses recovery Field data differs from training High / High ML developer collects labeled samples and limits claims The initial demonstrator accepts single-host downtime and HTTP access restricted to approved client IPs. Public production use requires a separate security and availability review, including HTTPS and authentication. CloudWatch logs and host metrics provide operational visibility but do not establish service availability or ML quality.
8 Expected outcomes Outcome Acceptance evidence Reproducible release Two image digests plus checkpoint map hashes and config Working AWS application Health and prediction succeed; browser prediction and explanation verified Secure artifact retrieval Private S3 GetObject by instance role with matching hashes Operational visibility Container logs, host metrics, and dashboard reviewed Documented recovery Rollback and EC2 stop/start rehearsal with observed timings Measured performance Latency report states image hardware concurrency samples and p95 Controlled cost Weekly gross-cost log and final cleanup evidence Success means a demonstrable and documented deployment within the approved spending envelope. It does not mean a proven agricultural diagnosis service, a zero-downtime platform or a completed twelve-week historical project. Accuracy and recovery objectives will be reported only after measurement.

AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026: Learning Beyond the Livestream Event: AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026: HCMC Watch Party
Date: September 29, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
Role: Attendee
I joined the HCMC watch party while the main AWS Cloud & AI Day event was taking place in Hanoi. More than 300 builders gathered to watch the sessions and discuss them together. I expected to spend most of the day following the livestream; I ended up learning just as much from the conversations between talks.
From AI features to AI systems The keynote connected three topics: agentic systems, data foundations, and cloud modernization. I had previously thought about an AI agent mostly as a model with tools. The discussion made me consider the parts around it: where its data comes from, what permissions it receives, and which existing business process it is meant to improve.
In the smaller roundtables, Solution Architects and developers spoke candidly about moving agents from proof-of-concept to production and managing cloud spend. That shifted my attention from whether an agent can complete a demo task to whether a team can operate it repeatedly, trace its actions, and justify its cost.
Lessons I am taking into my own work I want to add three checks to my next AI project: define the data sources and their quality, log the agent’s decisions and tool calls, and measure cost alongside task success. If an agent makes a workflow faster but creates hard-to-debug failures or unpredictable usage, the design still needs work.
This also connects with the current AI market. Adoption is broad, but useful deployment depends on dependable systems and clear value, not just adding an AI feature. Stanford HAI’s 2026 AI Index describes cost, reliability, and practical value as increasingly important competitive factors. I see those as engineering questions I can test on a small project: compare an AI-assisted workflow with a baseline, count failures, and track cost per completed task. Stanford HAI, 2026 AI Index.
The most valuable part of attending in person was being able to compare notes with other learners and practitioners. For my next event, I plan to arrive with a concrete question about measuring agent quality and leave with one experiment I can reproduce in my own project.

title: Blog 3
content:
Resolving Security Signals Faster with Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Agentic SOC Security teams rarely suffer from a shortage of alerts—they suffer from a shortage of triage capacity. Detection tools generate far more alerts than human analysts can investigate, and the same signal can mean completely different things depending on the environment: a password-guessing pattern might be an authorized penetration test in one account and an active credential-stuffing attack in another. Amazon GuardDuty flags unusual API activity, but does not tell you whether it is a real incident, a misconfiguration, or authorized testing.
This AWS Marketplace Blog post (co-authored with two writers from Arctic Wolf) explains how Arctic Wolf combines AI agents with its Concierge Security Team to turn raw AWS security findings into actionable decisions.
Core Architecture Components Aurora Agentic SOC: An AI-agent-driven security operations center built on the Aurora Superintelligence platform. Swarm of Experts: An agentic framework of specialized agents collaborating on triage, investigation, and response, with human analysts validating and taking over escalated cases. Concierge Security Team: Dedicated human specialists who understand the customer’s environment and act on their behalf. AWS Security Hub CSPM: Aggregates findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, AWS Config, and third-party tools into the standardized ASFF format. Amazon EventBridge + Amazon Data Firehose + Amazon S3 + AWS Lambda: An event-driven ingestion pipeline forwarding findings directly to the SOC. AWS CloudFormation: Templates provided by Arctic Wolf to deploy the entire ingestion pipeline inside the customer’s AWS account. Event-Driven Ingestion Flow The ingestion pipeline operates without polling—findings are pushed immediately as they appear:
AWS Security Hub CSPM normalizes incoming findings into ASFF. Amazon EventBridge emits an event whenever a new finding arrives. Amazon Data Firehose buffers and streams events into a landing S3 bucket, handling sudden incident spikes smoothly. AWS Lambda processes, enriches, and delivers the records into the destination S3 bucket. Arctic Wolf SOC reads the destination bucket via cross-account IAM delegation (no polling) and correlates findings with endpoint, network, and identity telemetry in Aurora. Beyond Security Hub, Arctic Wolf integrates with AWS CloudTrail, Amazon GuardDuty (single-account or multi-account via AWS Organizations / Control Tower), and AWS WAF, with over 120 alert rules reported across these integrations.
Human-Agent Division of Labor What stands out most is placing AI agents and humans in the roles where each excels: AI agents perform large-scale initial triage and correlation, while human experts handle complex judgment calls and customer communication. According to customer CloudHesive (cited in the post), reported outcomes included 50% fewer alerts requiring triage, 99% faster investigation-to-remediation, and 10× cost savings compared to the estimated cost of building an in-house SOC.
Caveats & Practical Notes Vendor-authored metrics: Because the article is co-authored by Arctic Wolf staff and closes with a subscription call-to-action, claims such as 10,000+ customers, 10+ trillion events per week, 14+ years of telemetry, and a 4.9/5 Gartner Peer Insights rating are vendor-provided without independent verification. Self-reported customer results: CloudHesive’s figures are customer-reported, and the 10× savings comparison is measured against an estimated in-house build cost rather than actual spend. Escalation logic not detailed: The article states that agents know when to stop and escalate to humans, but does not explain the mechanism or thresholds behind that decision. Pricing model: No list pricing is published. Arctic Wolf is procured via negotiated AWS Marketplace private offers (consolidated onto the AWS bill), while the in-account ingestion pipeline incurs standard AWS usage charges (estimable via the AWS Pricing Calculator). Prerequisites: Customers must enable AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty and hold an active Arctic Wolf subscription on AWS Marketplace. Teardown & offboarding: Removing the integration requires deleting the CloudFormation stacks (emptying any non-empty S3 buckets first) and notifying the Concierge team beforehand; deleting the stack only stops data ingestion and does not cancel the Marketplace subscription. Key Takeaway I read this article to explore a practical blueprint for security operations: let AI agents shoulder high-volume triage and initial correlation, while keeping business-context decisions firmly in human hands.
Source: Resolve security signals faster with Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Agentic SOC — Tim Sitze, Dan Jellesma, Kent Whitney, AWS Marketplace Blog (October 16, 2026)

title: Event 3
content:
Engineering in the AI Era: Reflections on Werner Vogels’ Keynote Event: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam
Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels, Amazon CTO
Date: October 2, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
Role: Attendee
I attended Dr. Werner Vogels’ keynote with a question many software students are asking: what should engineers learn as AI becomes part of everyday development? The talk did not frame engineering as a contest between people and AI. Instead, it returned to how teams understand workloads, design for failure, and take responsibility for systems.
Design from evidence, prepare for failure Vogels revisited the database pressure Amazon faced during a peak shopping period. The team examined actual request patterns and found that many operations were simple key-value lookups. That understanding helped motivate Dynamo, a design better matched to the workload and an ancestor of DynamoDB. I took this as a reminder to measure the problem before selecting fashionable technology.
He also discussed operational discipline: averages can hide poor experiences at the edge, and components will fail. Resilience therefore needs to be practiced, not assumed. For AI products, I think this applies to model and service failures too. A fallback path, clear error state, and a way to inspect outputs are part of the system, not optional extras.
My perspective as an AI student The description of the “Renaissance Developer” emphasized curiosity, systems thinking, ownership, breadth with depth, and communication. Those traits feel relevant as AI tools become common in coding. Generating code is getting easier; checking whether it is correct, safe, maintainable, and appropriate for the workload remains an engineering task.
I plan to review AI-generated code as carefully as code written by a teammate: understand each change, test edge cases, and document assumptions. I also want to map data flow through my projects and ask what happens when a model, API, or dependency fails. The WEF’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 lists AI and big data among the fastest-growing skill areas while also highlighting analytical thinking and collaboration. That combination matches what I took from the keynote: technical fluency matters, but judgment and communication determine how responsibly it is applied. World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025.
I left with a more practical goal than trying to predict which jobs AI will replace: become an engineer who can use AI tools, verify their work, and understand the system those tools help build.

Self Assessment 1 Skills demonstrated The work demonstrates separation of image delivery from deployment, artifact integrity verification, IAM role use, Docker runtime configuration and CloudWatch integration. Actual issues were resolved across Windows SSH key ACLs, missing instance credentials, incorrect S3 prefix or object access, and missing log-read permission. title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Sharing and Feedback Overall Evaluation 1. Learning experience The most valuable part of this internship has been working through a project that connects machine learning with cloud deployment. I began with tomato leaf images and a classification model, then worked on packaging the application and operating it on AWS. This helped me understand that a useful demonstration depends on more than model output: model files, class mapping, permissions, network access, logs, monitoring, cost and recovery all need attention.
2. Relevance to my major The project was relevant to my Information Technology studies and gave me a chance to apply programming and machine learning in a practical setting. It also introduced me to cloud operations that I had less experience with, including IAM roles, private S3 artifacts, Docker containers on EC2, CloudWatch logs and metrics, and secure web access.
3. Skills and professional growth Troubleshooting access, configuration and deployment issues taught me to verify each layer instead of assuming that a running page means the whole application works. Preparing worklogs, a workshop guide and technical blog posts also helped me explain technical decisions and limitations more clearly. Participating in cloud and AI community events gave me additional perspectives on system resilience, security, cost awareness and responsible use of AI.
4. Project challenges and lessons The project made the limits of a small demonstration clear. A single EC2 instance can become a point of failure, and host monitoring metrics do not prove that predictions are available or accurate. I also learned to distinguish a sample inference time from a proper performance measurement, and to avoid making claims about field accuracy without independent labeled data. In future work, I would plan acceptance checks and operational evidence alongside implementation from the start.
Additional Questions What did I find most satisfying?
Connecting the model and web application to AWS, then documenting the configuration and operational lessons, was the most satisfying part. It gave me a more complete view of how an AI feature moves from an experiment toward a usable service.
What could be improved for future interns?
A short milestone checklist with expected deliverables and acceptance criteria would help interns understand what evidence to collect at each stage. Regular review points for architecture, security and deployment would also help surface issues earlier while leaving room for interns to investigate and solve them.
Would I recommend the program to a friend?
Yes, especially to someone interested in cloud and AI who is ready to learn by building and documenting a practical project. A clear project scope and regular feedback would make that experience even more effective.
Suggestions and Expectations Provide a concise project-start guide covering scope, milestones, expected evidence and report structure. Include periodic mentor reviews at key stages, such as model integration, AWS permissions, public access and final acceptance. Share a cloud cost and cleanup checklist so interns can review running resources, budgets and end-of-project cleanup with confidence. Keep opportunities to present project results and exchange feedback with other interns or the AWS Study Group community. I hope to continue learning through hands-on cloud and AI projects, community knowledge sharing and feedback from experienced practitioners. I am grateful for the opportunity to build, troubleshoot and reflect on this project during the First Cloud AI Journey.

title: Introduction
content:
Introduction Introduction to Plant Disease Detection The Plant Disease Detection project is a learning and engineering demonstration of tomato leaf image classification. It connects a CPU-based image classifier to a web interface and a small AWS deployment. It is not validated for field diagnosis and should not be treated as advice for farmers or agronomists.
The application accepts JPEG or PNG images and returns ranked class predictions with model scores. These scores are not calibrated probabilities, and performance on the small external dataset does not establish reliability on field images.
Classification Scope & Target Classes The underlying neural network is trained to classify images into 11 distinct output classes, covering common bacterial, fungal, and viral infections in tomato leaves, as well as healthy controls and out-of-distribution inputs:
Class ID Disease / Category Name Pathogen / Condition Typical Visual Symptoms 0 Tomato___Bacterial_spot Xanthomonas campestris Small, water-soaked, dark spots with yellow halos 1 Tomato___Early_blight Alternaria solani Concentric target-like dark rings surrounded by chlorosis 2 Tomato___Late_blight Phytophthora infestans Irregular grayish-green water-soaked lesions on leaves 3 Tomato___Leaf_Mold Passalora fulva Pale green or yellow spots on upper surface, velvety olive mold below 4 Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot Septoria lycopersici Numerous circular spots with gray centers and dark margins 5 Tomato___Spider_mites Tetranychus urticae Yellow or white stippling, webbing on leaf undersides 6 Tomato___Target_Spot Corynespora casiicola Brown lesions with prominent concentric rings 7 Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus Geminivirus (Whitefly-borne) Upward curling, severe stunting, and bright interveinal chlorosis 8 Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus Tobamovirus Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns, leaf distortion 9 Tomato___healthy Control / Normal Vigorous green foliage free from chlorosis or necrotic tissue 10 unknown Out-of-Distribution Non-tomato foliage, corrupted images, or background noise [!NOTE] This is a learning, research, and deployment demonstration. It has not been validated for field diagnosis or commercial agronomic use.
Machine Learning Architecture: Knowledge Distillation The research compared several model architectures and includes a Knowledge Distillation experiment. This technique transfers information from a larger teacher model to a smaller student, but it does not guarantee better predictive performance:
graph TD Teacher["Teacher Model: ConvNeXt-Tiny<br/>(Heavyweight, High Capacity ~114 MiB)"] Student["Student Model: MobileNetV3-Small<br/>(Lightweight, CPU-Optimized ~6 MiB)"] Data["Tomato Leaf Dataset<br/>(Augmented Preprocessing)"] --> Teacher Data --> Student Teacher -->|Soft Probability Logits| KD_Loss["Knowledge Distillation Loss<br/>(KL Divergence + Cross-Entropy)"] Student -->|Student Predictions| KD_Loss KD_Loss -->|Backprop / Distill Knowledge| DistilledModel["Deployable Checkpoint:<br/>mobilenetv3_small_100_distilled_best.pth<br/>(Latency: 29.23 ms | Size: 6 MiB)"] Teacher Architecture (ConvNeXt-Tiny): Modern convolutional network with inverted bottlenecks, large 7x7 receptive fields, and superior feature extraction capabilities. Student Architecture (MobileNetV3-Small): Hardware-aware network search architecture utilizing hard-swish non-linearities and depthwise separable convolutions, optimized specifically for low-latency CPU execution. Recorded demo model: The distilled MobileNetV3 checkpoint is approximately 6 MiB. A single recorded CPU request took 29.23 ms for model inference; this is not a throughput or end-to-end latency result. Model quality varies across evaluation datasets, so this benchmark does not establish field reliability. Explainable AI (XAI) with Grad-CAM++ The application includes Grad-CAM++ (Generalized Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) as a visual aid for inspecting image regions associated with a prediction. A heatmap is an attribution visualization; it does not identify lesions or confirm a diagnosis.
Visual Comparison Across Architectures The following visualizations illustrate how different model architectures focus on distinct pathological features of the leaf:
Architecture Model Role Heatmap & Overlay Visualization MobileNetV3-Small Distilled AWS demo model ConvNeXt-Tiny Teacher Baseline EfficientNet-B0 Candidate Student Operational Pipeline on AWS The operational lifecycle connects code repository automation to AWS infrastructure:
CI Build and Manual Release: Pushes to master trigger GitHub Actions to run Python checks, build Next.js and publish container images to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). An operator deploys or rolls back a release on EC2 manually. Decoupled Checkpoint Storage: Model weights (model.pth) and class label mappings (class_to_idx.json) are maintained in a secure, private Amazon S3 bucket under the prefix mobilenet-distilled-v1/. Containerized EC2 Host: A single Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 instance pulls container images and mounts S3 model artifacts read-only into /app/artifacts. Networking & Ingress: The browser connects to the Next.js frontend on port 3000 and calls the FastAPI backend on port 8000 (/health, /predict, /explain) via the VPC Internet Gateway and Security Group rules restricted to approved source IPs (with CORS_ORIGINS configured). Observability: Container standard output and error streams are captured via the Docker awslogs driver into CloudWatch Logs. The CloudWatch Agent collects fine-grained host memory and disk utilization, reporting host metrics for review in the CloudWatch dashboard.

# Verify AWS identity aws sts get-caller-identity # Set default region to ap-southeast-2 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" aws configure set default.region ap-southeast-2 Step 2: EC2 Security Group Inbound Rules Create a dedicated Security Group named plant-disease-sg in your default VPC. Add the following inbound rules:
Type Protocol Port Range Source Description SSH TCP 22 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Administrative SSH shell access Custom TCP TCP 3000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Next.js Frontend Web Application Custom TCP TCP 8000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 FastAPI CPU Inference REST API Step 3: EC2 Instance Profile & IAM Permissions Attach an IAM Role to your EC2 instance so the application can read model artifacts from Amazon S3 and the CloudWatch Agent can publish host metrics without storing long-lived AWS credentials on the server. Operators need separate, scoped CloudWatch Logs read access to query logs from their own AWS CLI session.
Attach the following IAM policies to the role:
AmazonCloudWatchAgentServerPolicy (AWS Managed Policy): Allows the CloudWatch Agent to emit custom host metrics and create log streams. PlantDiseaseS3Policy (Inline Policy): Grants read-only access strictly to the model artifacts prefix: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowS3ModelArtifactsDownload", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2", "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2/mobilenet-distilled-v1/*" ] }, { "Sid": "AllowOperatorLogInspection", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:FilterLogEvents", "logs:GetLogEvents", "logs:DescribeLogStreams" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:ap-southeast-2:*:log-group:/plant-disease/*" } ] } Step 4: Provisioning EC2 Host Software Once logged into your EC2 instance via SSH, install Docker Engine and the CloudWatch Agent:
# Update Amazon Linux 2023 packages sudo dnf update -y # Install Docker and Git sudo dnf install -y docker git sudo systemctl enable --now docker sudo usermod -aG docker ec2-user # Install CloudWatch Agent sudo dnf install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # Verify installation docker --version aws --version

title: Architecture & Design
content:
Architecture & Design End-to-End System Architecture The Plant Disease Detection demonstration connects a machine-learning inference API to a web frontend and supporting AWS services in the Sydney (ap-southeast-2) region. Its architecture has four main parts: model artifact storage, CI image publishing, a two-container runtime on one EC2 host, and basic monitoring. It demonstrates selected MLOps and cloud engineering practices; it does not provide validated agricultural diagnostics or an automated production release process.
Model Checkpoint & Artifact Storage Pipeline (Amazon S3 → EC2 Host): Securely decouples multi-megabyte neural network weights from application container images, verifying cryptographic integrity at runtime. CI Image Build and Publishing (GitHub Actions → GHCR): Runs automated checks and publishes frontend and API images; an operator deploys releases to EC2 manually. Web Application & Model Inference (Single EC2 Host): Runs a responsive Next.js frontend and a PyTorch CPU FastAPI service with an optional Grad-CAM++ visualization. Operations, Observability & Security: Uses least-privilege AWS IAM instance profiles, client-restricted Security Groups, CloudWatch Logs, custom host memory and disk metrics, and a monitoring dashboard. graph LR Dev["Developer"] -->|push to master| CI["GitHub Actions: tests, builds, smoke checks"] CI -->|publish images| GHCR["GHCR"] Model["Model artifacts"] -->|upload| S3["Private S3"] GHCR -->|manual pull| EC2["Single EC2 host: Next.js + FastAPI"] S3 -->|manual download + hash check| EC2 Browser["Browser"] -->|HTTP: 3000 / 8000| EC2 EC2 -->|container logs + host metrics| CW["CloudWatch logs + dashboard"] End-to-End Operational Lifecycle & Sequence Flow The interaction sequence across the nine steps in the architecture flow below is detailed below:
Step # Subsystem / Boundary Source Component Destination Component Protocol / Mechanism Technical Action & Description ① Client Ingress Users / Browser VPC / Internet Gateway HTTP :3000 / :8000 Approved client IPs access web UI and API ports through the VPC Internet Gateway and Security Group (TCP 22, 3000, 8000). ② Web Frontend Internet Gateway frontend Container (EC2) GET :3000 (UI) Serves the Next.js standalone UI (node server.js) running as a non-root user. ③ AI Inference API Internet Gateway / Browser backend Container (EC2) POST :8000 (API) FastAPI + Uvicorn (1 worker) exposes /health, /predict, /explain using MobileNetV3-Small (KD) on CPU (2 threads, 1 slot) with /app/artifacts mounted read-only (ro). ④ Source Control & CI Developer (also operator) GitHub (master branch) git push → trigger Pushing to master triggers GitHub Actions (pytest · build · smoke). ⑤ Container Publishing GitHub Actions GHCR publish CI builds and publishes digest-pinned api and frontend container images to GitHub Container Registry. ⑥ Manual Deployment GHCR Amazon EC2 (AL2023 x86_64) docker pull @sha256 digest Operator manually pulls immutable container images over SSH and recreates the containers on EC2. ⑦ Offline Training Upload Local Workstation Amazon S3 (Private Bucket) upload Training & audit workflow (audit_models.py, Kaggle tomato set) uploads mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth (~6 MiB) and class_to_idx.json (no VPC endpoint). ⑧ Artifact Retrieval Amazon S3 EC2 Host → backend aws s3 cp + sha256 EC2 uses its AWS IAM instance profile (no static keys) to download weights, verify SHA256 hashes, and mount /app/artifacts (ro). ⑨ Logging & Telemetry EC2 Containers & CloudWatch Agent Amazon CloudWatch awslogs + host metrics Containers stream awslogs and CloudWatch Agent reports mem + disk every 60 s. Architectural Principles & Subsystem Breakdown Subsystem 1: Decoupled Weights from Code In enterprise MLOps, embedding multi-megabyte binary checkpoints directly into container images causes significant operational anti-patterns: base images swell to several gigabytes, build and push cycles stall, and minor weight updates require a complete container rebuild.
The architecture decouples application runtime code from model checkpoints:
Compact Application Images: The Docker image packages solely runtime code, library dependencies (FastAPI, PyTorch CPU, Next.js), and static templates. Dedicated Cloud Storage: Model checkpoints reside securely in a private S3 bucket (plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2) under prefix mobilenet-distilled-v1/. Read-Only Container Mount: During deployment, the host pulls the model artifacts via IAM role permissions, audits SHA256 hashes, and mounts /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1 as a read-only volume (/app/artifacts:ro) into the FastAPI container. Subsystem 2: Continuous Integration & Immutable Delivery Every push to the master branch triggers an automated GitHub Actions workflow (pytest · build · smoke):
PyTest Schema & Transform Suite: Validates input tensor normalization, PIL image decoding, and JSON response contracts. Next.js Standalone Optimization & Smoke Tests: Compiles TypeScript, packages a minimal Node.js 22 server, and runs container smoke checks. Digest-Pinned Images: Images (api + frontend) are published to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) and pulled manually over SSH onto EC2 by immutable digest hash (@sha256:f61be157... and @sha256:ec211d13...), preventing mutable tag discrepancies. Subsystem 3: Containerized Web & Model Inference The compute layer runs on an Amazon Linux 2023 (x86_64) EC2 instance hosting two isolated containers:
Next.js Standalone Frontend (:3000): Runs node server.js as low-privilege non-root user nextjs (UID 1001), serving responsive mobile and desktop client interfaces. FastAPI Backend (:8000): Python 3.12 + Uvicorn (1 worker) exposing /health, /predict, and /explain, with PyTorch CPU intra-op thread allocation restricted to 2 cores (MODEL_THREADS=2) and a single bounded execution slot (1 slot) to prevent CPU saturation. MobileNetV3-Small Distilled: The demo checkpoint is approximately 6 MiB. A recorded single-request CPU inference measured 29.23 ms; this measurement is not a throughput or full-request latency result, and evaluation results do not establish field accuracy. Grad-CAM++ Visualization: The /explain endpoint returns a heatmap and overlay as an aid for inspecting the model response. These visualizations do not segment lesions or verify a diagnosis. Subsystem 4: Operations, Least-Privilege Security & Observability AWS IAM Instance Profile: Instance role with no static access keys, scoped to s3:GetObject on the model bucket and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy. Amazon VPC & Security Groups: Inbound firewall restricts ports 22 (SSH), 3000 (Web UI), and 8000 (API) exclusively to approved source IPs (/32). Amazon CloudWatch Logs: Captures stdout and stderr streams with a 7-day retention policy to prevent disk saturation while maintaining troubleshooting history. Amazon CloudWatch Agent: Collects host memory and disk metrics under namespace PlantDisease/Host; CloudWatch Logs stores both containers’ output and the dashboard provides an operational view. Model Artifact Boundary The checkpoint and class map are stored in a private S3 bucket rather than inside the application image. During a manual release, the operator downloads both files, verifies their SHA256 hashes, and mounts the directory read-only into the API container. The download and verification commands are part of the deployment procedure in 5.4.
The current demo reaches the regional S3 endpoint through its public subnet route. A private S3 VPC endpoint is a possible later network enhancement and is not part of the deployed configuration.

title: Deployment Strategy
content:
Deployment Strategy 5.4.1 CI Build and Image Publishing Pushes to master trigger the automated continuous integration (CI) workflow in GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml):
Python unit and API tests, including model transforms and prediction schemas. Next.js production builds, ensuring static asset optimization, TypeScript type safety, and non-root runtime compatibility. Multi-stage Docker image packaging for the frontend and inference API, followed by publishing to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). The workflow does not deploy to EC2; release deployment and rollback are performed manually. Recorded Release Provenance To guarantee reproducibility and avoid mutable tag discrepancies (such as :latest), the deployment recorded immutable git commit hashes and image digests:
Component Target Version / Identifier Recorded Digest Hash Git Commit ff6b75bf3a625db124cc6449f52fa224bf76631e Validated release baseline Backend API Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-detection-api sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c Frontend Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-detection-frontend sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.2 Retrieve and Verify Model Artifacts Before starting the API container, confirm that the EC2 instance has assumed its IAM role, then download the checkpoint and class map from the private S3 bucket:
# Verify the EC2 instance profile identity and set the deployment region aws sts get-caller-identity export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" read -r -p "Enter S3 bucket name: " MODEL_BUCKET # Download model weights and class map mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1 aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth" /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1/model.pth aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/class_to_idx.json" /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json # Verify SHA256 checksums sha256sum /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1/model.pth /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json The downloaded files must match the release hashes:
Artifact Expected SHA256 Approximate size model.pth 05e72798a74193499f17c4c8267c1436e8bc65cc1e8b8037245664a17644efa5 ~6.0 MiB class_to_idx.json ff5c73e7a7e3e495593fa664b75ebc73de4c9a425f1d847351ae60bc1fbaa786 ~1.2 KiB [!IMPORTANT] If a hash differs, stop the release and check that the files belong to the same model version. The API reports the model as unavailable if required artifacts are missing or invalid.
[!NOTE] This demo downloads artifacts through the public subnet’s route to the regional S3 endpoint. A private S3 VPC endpoint is a possible future network change, not part of the current setup.
5.4.3 Configure Backend Runtime The backend container runs a FastAPI application under Python 3.12 with PyTorch CPU. The host mounts the previously downloaded checkpoints/v1 directory as a read-only volume at /app/artifacts.
Start the backend container with the following configuration:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-api \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1:/app/artifacts:ro \ -e MODEL_CHECKPOINT=/app/artifacts/model.pth \ -e MODEL_CLASS_MAP=/app/artifacts/class_to_idx.json \ -e MODEL_NAME=mobilenetv3_small_100 \ -e MODEL_THREADS=2 \ -e CORS_ORIGINS="http://localhost:3000,http://$(curl -s http://checkip.amazonaws.com):3000" \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/backend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-detection-api@sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c [!NOTE]
MODEL_THREADS=2 restricts PyTorch intra-op parallelism to 2 CPU cores, preventing inference requests from overwhelming the host OS. The application initializes the neural network weights strictly once at process startup. If weights are missing, corrupt, or incompatible, /health reports status unavailable and API calls return 503. 5.4.4 Configure Frontend and Networking The frontend is packaged using a multi-stage Docker build producing a Next.js Standalone server running on Node.js 22, matching the frontend Dockerfile. The container runs as a dedicated non-root nextjs user and listens on port 3000.
Start the frontend container:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-frontend \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3000:3000 \ -e NODE_ENV=production \ -e PORT=3000 \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/frontend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-detection-frontend@sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.5 Validate Application Behavior Verify that both containers are running healthy, then execute health checks and a test prediction using the fixture leaf image:
# 1. Check running containers sudo docker ps # 2. Check Backend Health curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 3. Check Frontend HTTP Header curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000 # 4. Perform Live Inference with Fixture Image curl --fail-with-body \ -F "file=@frontend/tests/fixtures/tomato-leaf.jpg;type=image/jpeg" \ -F "top_k=3" \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict Recorded Verification Results The table below documents the empirical test results recorded on the Sydney EC2 deployment:

title: Monitoring & Security
content:
Monitoring & Security 5.5.1 Container Logging & Host Metrics Collection The demonstration’s basic observability uses Amazon CloudWatch Logs and the Amazon CloudWatch Agent:
1. Container Structured Logging The Docker daemon uses the awslogs log driver to stream all stdout and stderr output directly to dedicated CloudWatch Log Groups:
/plant-disease/backend: Captures structured JSON middleware access logs, including request_id, client IP, HTTP method, request path, status code, and execution duration. /plant-disease/frontend: Captures Next.js server requests, static file requests, and rendering errors. Log Retention: Set to 7 days to minimize storage overhead while preserving troubleshooting history. Inspect real-time application logs using the AWS CLI:
# Stream the last 10 minutes of backend API logs aws logs tail /plant-disease/backend --since 10m --region ap-southeast-2 # Filter for errors or warnings aws logs filter-log-events \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --filter-pattern "ERROR" \ --region ap-southeast-2 2. CloudWatch Agent Metrics While standard EC2 monitoring provides hypervisor-level CPU utilization, memory and disk metrics are not visible from the hypervisor. The Amazon CloudWatch Agent is configured on the host to collect and report memory and disk telemetry every 60 seconds under the custom namespace PlantDisease/Host:
Create /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json:
{ "metrics": { "namespace": "PlantDisease/Host", "metrics_collected": { "mem": { "measurement": [ "mem_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 }, "disk": { "measurement": [ "disk_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60, "resources": [ "/" ] } } } } Start the CloudWatch Agent service and verify status. The current deployment also provides the plant-disease-demo CloudWatch dashboard for reviewing host metrics alongside logs:
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json # Check agent status sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a status 5.5.2 Security Hardening & Least Privilege The demonstration applies a small set of access and runtime controls:
graph TD subgraph Security Controls Applied P1["S3 Private Bucket: Block All Public Access enabled"] P2["IAM Instance Profile: No static access keys"] P3["Security Group: Ingress locked to approved source IPs /32"] P4["Container Isolation: Read-Only volume mounts"] P5["Non-Root Execution: User nextjs & appuser"] end Private S3 Bucket: S3 Block Public Access is completely enabled. Model weights are accessible solely by authenticated requests bearing the EC2 instance’s assumed IAM role. Elimination of Long-Lived Credentials: No access keys, secret keys, or private SSH keys are stored in source control or on the server file system. Read-Only Container Mounts: The model weights directory /app/artifacts is mounted into the container with the :ro flag, ensuring the inference engine cannot mutate model checkpoints. Non-Root Execution: The container images run under dedicated low-privilege system accounts (nextjs UID 1001 for frontend, appuser for backend).

title: Operations & Cleanup
content:
Operations & Cleanup Daily Operational Routine In a learning, research, or proof-of-concept environment, continuous 24/7 EC2 execution accumulates unnecessary hourly compute costs. Establish a disciplined routine for pausing and resuming workloads:
1. Pausing Applications Between Sessions When halting daily development, pause the container runtime and stop the underlying EC2 instance:
# On EC2 Host via SSH: Gracefully stop application containers sudo docker stop plant-disease-frontend plant-disease-api # From Operator Terminal or AWS CloudShell: Stop the EC2 instance aws ec2 stop-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 [!NOTE] Stopping an EC2 instance halts hourly EC2 compute billing. Attached Amazon EBS root volumes, stored CloudWatch metrics, and S3 objects remain intact but continue to incur standard low-cost storage fees.
2. Resuming Operations When resuming work, restart the instance and initialize services in the correct dependency sequence:
# 1. Start EC2 instance aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Reconnect via SSH (Note: Public IPv4 may change unless using an Elastic IP) ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@<NEW_PUBLIC_IP> # 3. Start Backend first and await readiness sudo docker start plant-disease-api curl --retry 5 --retry-connrefused http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 4. Start Frontend sudo docker start plant-disease-frontend [!IMPORTANT] If your EC2 instance does not have an allocated Elastic IP (EIP), stopping and restarting the instance assigns a new public IPv4 address. You must update your SSH connection string, client browser URL, and backend CORS_ORIGINS setting accordingly.
Remove Demo Resources and Review Remaining Costs At the end of the workshop, remove resources created specifically for this demo, then review the AWS Billing console for remaining charges. This checklist does not delete unrelated account resources or guarantee that the account’s total bill will be zero.
graph TD Step1["1. Terminate the demo EC2 instance"] Step2["2. Delete CloudWatch log groups and dashboard"] Step3["3. Empty and delete the dedicated model bucket"] Step4["4. Release the demo Elastic IP, if allocated"] Step5["5. Review leftover volumes, snapshots, and billable resources"] Step1 --> Step2 Step2 --> Step3 Step3 --> Step4 Step4 --> Step5 Step-by-Step Deletion Commands: # 1. Terminate the EC2 instance aws ec2 terminate-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Delete CloudWatch Log Groups aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --region ap-southeast-2 aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/frontend \ --region ap-southeast-2 aws cloudwatch delete-dashboards \ --dashboard-names plant-disease-demo \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 3. Empty and delete S3 Bucket # This command removes current objects. If bucket versioning is enabled, # remove prior object versions using the S3 console before deleting the bucket. aws s3 rm "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET" --recursive aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$MODEL_BUCKET" --region ap-southeast-2 # 4. Release Elastic IP (if allocated) aws ec2 release-address --allocation-id "$EIP_ALLOC_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 # 5. List available EBS volumes and your account's snapshots for review. # Delete only resources confirmed to belong to this demo; do not bulk-delete. aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available --region ap-southeast-2 aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self --region ap-southeast-2 [!WARNING] Confirm the EC2 instance, S3 bucket, and Elastic IP belong to this demo before deleting them. aws s3 rm --recursive does not remove previous object versions from a versioned bucket. After cleanup, review EBS volumes and snapshots, then check billing for resources that remain in use.

[1] Project Repository & Release Artifacts: starkkk1/plant-disease-detection — Complete training notebooks, model export scripts, and Next.js / FastAPI source code. [2] AWS EC2 Stop and Start Lifecycle: AWS Documentation on Instance Lifecycle — Details on state preservation, ephemeral storage behavior, and public IP reassignments. [3] Amazon S3 HeadObject and Least-Privilege IAM: S3 Security Best Practices — Policy scoping for model weight downloads and bucket isolation. [4] Amazon CloudWatch Agent Installation: CloudWatch Agent User Guide — Custom metrics collection for host RAM and disk percent.
